details:
**"Paul Revere's Ride"**
Longfellow's most famous poem, which begins "Listen, my children, and you shall hear / Of the midnight ride of Paul Revere" and is set "on the eighteenth of April, in Seventy-five." The silversmith Revere waits for a signal from the belfry of the Old North Church, rides to spread the "cry of alarm / To every Middlesex village and farm," and delivers a "midnight message" that "the people will waken and listen to hear." It was published in Tales of a Wayside Inn and is the near-universal giveaway.

**"One if by land, and two if by sea"**
The line describing the lantern signal hung in the Old North Church tower in "Paul Revere's Ride"; two lanterns mean the British are crossing by water. The poem takes liberties with history: the real Revere was captured near Lexington and never reached "the bridge in Concord town."

**The Song of Hiawatha**
Longfellow's 1855 epic about an Ojibwe hero, set "By the shores of Gitche Gumee, / By the shining Big-Sea-Water" (Lake Superior). It is written in trochaic tetrameter, a meter Longfellow borrowed from the Finnish epic Kalevala, and has sections such as "The Four Winds" and "The White Man's Foot."

**Minnehaha**
Hiawatha's beloved and wife, the "Laughing Water," whose wooing and marriage are a central plotline of The Song of Hiawatha. She dies of fever and hunger during a terrible winter famine, one of the poem's most famous episodes.

**Nokomis, Wenonah, and Mudjekeewis**
Hiawatha's family in The Song of Hiawatha. His grandmother Nokomis fell to earth from the full moon; her daughter Wenonah was seduced by Mudjekeewis, the West Wind, and gave birth to Hiawatha. Hiawatha later fights his father Mudjekeewis, and also kills the magician Pearl-Feather after passing the Kenabeek serpents. The section on the winds also tells how Shawondasee, the South Wind, fell in love with a dandelion he mistook for a golden-haired maiden.

**Evangeline, A Tale of Acadie**
Longfellow's 1847 narrative poem in dactylic hexameter, which opens "This is the forest primeval. The murmuring pines and the hemlocks." It follows an Acadian girl from the village of Grand-Pré whose people are expelled from Nova Scotia by the British in 1755.

**Gabriel Lajeunesse**
Evangeline's fiancé, separated from her during the expulsion of the Acadians. Evangeline searches for him across America for years and finally finds him, old and dying in an almshouse during an epidemic, in Philadelphia, where she works as a Sister of Mercy.

**"The Wreck of the Hesperus"**
A ballad in which a skipper ignores warnings (including a "golden ring" around the moon) and sails into a winter storm. He ties his young daughter to the mast to keep her from being swept away, but the schooner, named for the evening star, is wrecked "on the reef of Norman's Woe" and she is found dead, still lashed to the mast. In the poem she thinks "of Christ, who stilled the wave, / On the Lake of Galilee."

**"The Cross of Snow"**
A sonnet mourning Longfellow's second wife, Frances "Fanny" Appleton, who died in 1861 after her dress caught fire; Longfellow was burned trying to save her and grew his famous beard to hide the scars. It describes "a soul more white / Never through martyrdom of fire was led / To its repose" and ends with "the cross I wear upon my breast," comparing his grief to a cross of snow on a mountain that stays "changeless" through the seasons. It was found among his papers after his death.

**"The Village Blacksmith"**
A poem that opens "Under a spreading chestnut-tree / The village smithy stands." The blacksmith has "large and sinewy hands," hair "crisp, and black, and long," and goes on "toiling,—rejoicing,—sorrowing" through life, serving as a model of honest labor.

**"The Children's Hour"**
A domestic poem in which the speaker hears "the patter of little feet" as his three daughters, "Grave Alice, and laughing Allegra, / And Edith with golden hair," ambush him in his study. He calls them "blue-eyed banditti" and says he will keep them forever "in the dungeon / In the round-tower of my heart."

**The Courtship of Miles Standish**
A narrative poem set in early Plymouth Colony. The shy Puritan captain Miles Standish sends his friend John Alden to propose to Priscilla Mullins for him, and she replies, "Why don't you speak for yourself, John?" Alden and Priscilla eventually marry.

**Tales of a Wayside Inn**
A collection framed like The Canterbury Tales, beginning "One Autumn night, in Sudbury town," in which a group of travelers at an inn tell stories. It includes "Paul Revere's Ride" (the Landlord's Tale), "The Saga of King Olaf" about a Viking king, and the source of the phrase "ships that pass in the night."

**"A Psalm of Life"**
An inspirational poem that rejects the idea that "Life is but an empty dream," declaring "Life is real! Life is earnest! / And the grave is not its goal." It urges readers to leave "footprints on the sands of time."

**"The Skeleton in Armor" and "Excelsior"**
Two other short poems used as clues. "The Skeleton in Armor" was inspired by a skeleton found in Massachusetts believed to be a Viking's; the Viking ghost tells how he eloped with a "blue-eyed maid," fled to America, cried "Skoal!", and killed himself after she died. In "Excelsior," a youth climbs the Alps carrying a "banner with the strange device" and is found frozen to death, still grasping it. Longfellow also made the first American translation of Dante's Divine Comedy.
